headline: US futures tick higher on renewed US-Iran ceasefire while tech mega-caps remain under pressure from AI cost concerns and a data-heavy week looms.
stance: Cautiously constructive, with a clear sector split. The broad market held its ground on Friday — S&P 500 prior cash close 7,354.02, Dow 51,876.11, Nasdaq 25,297.62 — as investors rotated out of AI mega-caps into industrials, healthcare, and cyclicals. Overnight, S&P 500 futures are trading near 7,457 and Nasdaq 100 futures near ~29,728 (both OVERNIGHT/PRE-MARKET levels), a modest lift driven by Washington and Tehran agreeing to halt renewed hostilities. The core risk this week is the Fed hike narrative: markets are pricing meaningful odds of a December hike and the dollar is near a one-year high, compressing the equity risk premium; a CAPE of 40.7 offers no margin for error if yields re-accelerate.

news.head: US-Iran halt renewed strikes
news.body: Washington and Tehran agreed to suspend fresh hostilities after a flare-up of tit-for-tat strikes — including an Iranian attack on a cargo vessel near Oman — that threatened to derail the 14-point interim peace accord signed in mid-June; Doha talks are set to resume this week.

news.head: AI cost fears hammer tech
news.body: Mega-cap tech ended a fifth losing week as Apple and Microsoft announced price increases, OpenAI reportedly considered delaying its IPO, and investors questioned whether spiraling AI infrastructure costs justify current valuations — the Nasdaq shed roughly 2%+ on the week.

news.head: PCE in-line, Fed hike odds sticky
news.body: The May PCE inflation report came in broadly as expected, prompting investors to modestly pare rate-hike bets, but markets still price roughly 80% odds of a Fed hike by December under Chair Warsh, keeping the dollar near a one-year high.

news.head: Oil back near pre-war levels
news.body: WTI crude (prior cash close $70.24/bbl) and Brent ($73.57/bbl) have retreated sharply on peace-deal optimism, though energy supply chains remain disrupted — over 11,000 seafarers were still stuck in the Persian Gulf as of last week.

news.head: Micron beats but chip wedge widens
news.body: Micron reported strong results, yet the earnings did not lift the broader semiconductor complex, underscoring that good chip earnings are not sufficient to reverse macro-driven AI valuation re-rating.

news.head: Gold slides off highs
news.body: Gold (prior cash close $4,103/oz) has pulled back toward ~$4,040–$4,051 in overnight trading (OVERNIGHT/PRE-MARKET), down roughly 1%–2% from Friday's close, as de-escalation in the Middle East reduces safe-haven demand and the dollar holds firm.

news.head: Data-heavy week ahead
news.body: June 29 has no major scheduled releases; June 30 brings consumer confidence, JOLTS, and Nike/Constellation Brands earnings; July 1 delivers ADP payrolls, ISM Manufacturing PMI, and construction spending.

implications: Overnight futures gains (~+0.5% S&P, ~+0.7% Nasdaq — OVERNIGHT/PRE-MARKET) are geopolitical relief, not a fundamental re-rating; the AI valuation overhang and Fed hike risk remain intact.

Falling oil (WTI near $70, Brent near $73 — PRIOR CASH CLOSE) is a genuine disinflationary tailwind that has already nudged the 10-year yield below 4.5% intra-week — watch whether it holds at the prior cash close 4.38%.
Quarter-end rebalancing (today is the last Monday of Q2) may add cross-current volatility as funds trim equity winners and reinstate fixed-income exposure.

The rotation out of mega-cap tech into industrials, healthcare, and small-caps is corroborated by breadth: 65.7% of S&P 500 stocks trade above their 50-day average, but only 49.5% of Nasdaq 100 stocks do — the index is being carried by fewer names.

Positioning: Speculators have almost no bullish bets left in Nasdaq 100 futures (bottom 4th percentile of 3 years) and Russell 2000 futures (bottom 2nd percentile) — a contrarian floor that historically limits downside and sets up squeeze risk on any catalyst. Copper speculators, however, are piled into longs at the 95th percentile — a contrarian warning for industrial metals. British Pound specs are washed out (1st percentile), a contrarian-bullish lean for GBP.

watch.head: JOLTS + consumer confidence (Jun 30)
watch.body: May job openings and June consumer confidence will be the first hard data points of the week; any upside surprise in openings keeps September hike odds alive and pressures rate-sensitive equities.

watch.head: USD/JPY intervention risk
watch.body: The yen (prior cash close 161.73 ¥/$) sits at the 99.7th percentile of its 3-year range — an extreme historically associated with Japanese Ministry of Finance intervention; a sudden yen strengthening would unwind carry trades and spike volatility.

watch.head: ISM Manufacturing (Jul 1)
watch.body: The last reading was 54.0 (expanding); a miss toward 50 would corroborate softening demand and ease Fed hike bets, supporting bonds and rate-sensitive sectors.

watch.head: Copper at extreme
watch.body: Copper (prior cash close $6.1975/lb, 96th percentile) is priced for perfection in global growth; a disappointment in Chinese data or ISM could trigger a sharp unwind given heavily crowded speculator longs.

watch.head: Fed speakers + Warsh tone
watch.body: Any signal from Fed Chair Warsh this week on the pace of potential hikes relative to the still-elevated PCE will set the yield and dollar trajectory into Q3.

sections.title: Macro & Rates
bullets: 10-year Treasury yield prior cash close 4.38%, 2-year at 4.07% — the curve is a slim +31 bps positive, its steepest in this cycle, signaling markets see eventual easing but not imminently.
Real rates (inflation-adjusted 10-year yield) stand at 2.18% — historically tight for equity multiples, compressing the case for paying 40.7x cyclically-adjusted earnings (CAPE).
The 10-year breakeven inflation rate is 2.20% — well-anchored, suggesting the bond market trusts the Fed's resolve even as nominal yields stay elevated.
Financial conditions indexes (ANFCI –0.477, STLFSI –0.96) remain loose — i.e., money is still flowing freely through the system — which has cushioned equities so far.
The dollar index (DXY) prior cash close 101.37 is near a one-year high, pressured by rate-hike pricing; a stronger dollar tightens conditions for emerging markets and multinationals.
Bank reserves ($2,951bn) remain ample; the Treasury General Account ($918.7bn) is large and reverse repo ($6.4bn) near zero — net liquidity conditions are not tightening sharply from plumbing.
Term premium on the 10-year is 75.2 bps — investors are demanding extra compensation to hold long bonds, limiting the Fed's capacity to engineer easy conditions via the curve alone.
sections.positioning: Speculators have almost no bullish bets left in 3M SOFR futures (1st percentile of 3 years) — a contrarian-bullish lean for short-term rates, meaning the market is priced for maximum Fed hawkishness in the near term.

sections.title: Equity Markets
bullets: S&P 500 prior cash close 7,354.02; Dow 51,876.11; Nasdaq Composite 25,297.62 — all indices ended a losing week as tech led the selloff.
Overnight S&P 500 futures near ~7,457 and Nasdaq 100 futures near ~29,728 (OVERNIGHT/PRE-MARKET) — modest relief rally on ceasefire news.

Breadth is surprisingly healthy: 65.7% of S&P 500 stocks trade above their 50-day moving average and 64.2% above their 200-day — the index weakness is concentrated in a handful of large-cap tech names, not broad deterioration.
The Nasdaq 100 tells a different story: only 49.5% of its components trade above their 50-day average, reflecting just how much of the index's recent weakness stems from AI mega-cap repricing.
VIX prior cash close 18.41 — fear is modest; VXN (Nasdaq-specific volatility) at 30.82 is meaningfully higher, confirming that the stress is tech-specific, not market-wide.
SKEW at 139.4 — sophisticated investors are paying up for tail-risk protection (put options far below current prices), suggesting an undercurrent of caution beneath the calm VIX surface.
Equity-credit correlation is 0.755 — stocks and credit spreads are moving together tightly, meaning any deterioration in credit would likely drag equities quickly.

The equity risk premium (ERP) is –2.05% — stocks are priced to yield less than bonds on a risk-adjusted basis, the weakest valuation cushion in years; this is a structural headwind, not a day-to-day trigger, but it limits upside conviction.
Rotation is the story: industrials led Thursday's session (+2.19%), healthcare and materials also gained, while consumer discretionary fell 1.78% — classic late-cycle defensive rotation.
sections.positioning: Speculator net positioning in Nasdaq 100 futures is at the 4th percentile of 3 years and Russell 2000 futures at the 2nd percentile — speculators have almost no bullish bets left, a contrarian floor that raises squeeze risk on any positive catalyst. VIX futures specs are also near lows (12th percentile), another contrarian-bullish lean for equities.

single_name.note: Six Flags Entertainment (Consumer Cyclical) — large off-exchange block buying (quiet institutional accumulation) and a burst of unusual options buying are live; shorts are heavy at 9.16 days-to-cover (squeeze risk elevated); company insiders have been buying; stock trades above its 200-day moving average. Fits the rotation-into-cyclicals theme as AI cost fears push money toward domestic leisure.

sections.title: Credit & Liquidity
bullets: HY-IG spread ratio at 278 bps (as of Jun 25) and IG OAS at 76 bps — credit spreads are not flashing systemic stress, consistent with the loose financial conditions readings.
Commercial paper funding spread (CPFF) at 19 bps and FRA-OIS / SOFR-OIS each at 1 bp — interbank funding markets are essentially frictionless; no 2008-style liquidity crunch signals.
Bank credit growth is +6.3% YoY (as of Jun 17) — healthy enough to support the economy but not inflationary; loan syndication rates at 6.94% reflect higher-for-longer pass-through.
M2 money supply is growing +5.58% YoY (as of May) and the Fed balance sheet +1.1% YoY — not tightening aggressively, which explains why financial conditions remain loose despite high rates.
SLOOS survey shows 8.1% of banks tightening standards on commercial/industrial loans and only 2% on commercial real estate (as of Apr) — credit availability remains broadly supportive.
sections.positioning: Primary dealers' high-yield bond inventory is at the 89th percentile of its 3-year range — dealers are crowded long high-yield, a contrarian warning that HY credit could face selling pressure if risk appetite fades.

single_name.note: Matador Resources (Energy) — large off-exchange block buying and a burst of unusual options buying are live; company insiders have been buying (2 rules fired); 7.64 days-to-cover means shorts are heavy with meaningful squeeze risk; stock is above its 200-day line. With oil near $70/bbl and HY energy credit still functioning, this is a levered way to play any oil floor.
